parole.significato: Used to form regular plurals of nouns that end in certain suffixes or syllables, such as -el, -er, -en, -em, -eur, -aar…
parole.testo: Unknown. Not present in Old Dutch, which used -a from Proto-Germanic *-ōz as the plural ending. Possibly spread from Middle Low German -s, -es, from Old Saxon -os, -as, from Proto-Germanic *-ōs. Further etymology is unknown, but cognate with Old English -as (English -s).

parole.significato: the part of a cow stable's floor on which the cows' hindlegs stand
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bôs, from Old Saxon *bōs, from Proto-West Germanic *bans, from Proto-Germanic *bansaz (“barn, stall (for animals)”).

parole.significato: the spoil, booty taken by violence, as in war
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Middle Low German büte, whence also German Beute and eventually all other related forms. Of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly a Celtic borrowing, from Proto-Celtic *boudi (“victory, booty, spoils”). If so, related to the name of Boudica, a British Celtic queen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German dāler, from German Taler, a shortening of Joachimsthaler and Schlickenthaler.
Perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Equivalent to deft + -ig. Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *daftī (“fitting, suitable”).

parole.significato: down, small bird feathers used as insulation material in covers and sleeping bags
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch donst or Middle Low German dūne, all from Old Norse dúnn.
Borrowed from Middle Low German drīste, from Old Saxon thrīsti, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīstī.
From Middle Low German drōs, of uncertain origin, but possibly related to sense 2 (“strangles”).
From Middle Dutch eigenwijs, probably from Middle Low German eigenwīs.
From Middle Dutch etstoel, perhaps from Middle Low German [Term?]. Equivalent to ette (“judge”) + stoel (“chair”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German flink (“quick, gleaming”). Perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *flakurōną (“to flutter, beat repeatedly”). Compare also Middle Dutch vlinken (verb).

Frequentative of gabben (compare Swedish begabba (“to mock”)), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German gabben (“to joke, make fun of”), from Proto-Germanic *gappon-, *gabbōn- (“to joke”), probably related to the root of gapen (“to gape”).
From Middle Low German *gammel, from Old Saxon *gamal, from Proto-West Germanic *gamal, from Proto-Germanic *gamalaz (“old”). Doublet of gamel.
Borrowed in the 16th century from Middle Low German grense, grenitse and/or German Grenze, both ultimately from Old Polish granica, from Proto-Slavic *granica.
Borrowed from Middle Low German grînen, from Old Saxon *grīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *grīnan (“to snarl”). Doublet of grijnen.
From Middle Dutch hacke, from Middle Low German hakke, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hak(k)-, perhaps related to *hakô. Cognate with German Hacke.
From Middle Low German hump, from Old Saxon *hump (“hill, heap, thick piece”), from Proto-Germanic *humpaz (“hip, height”), from Proto-Indo-European *kumb- (“curved”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German juften, from Russian юфть (juftʹ).

parole.significato: bottom of a ship: the keel
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kiel, probably borrowed from Middle Low German kēl, Middle English kele, or Middle French quille, ultimately from Old Norse kjǫlr, from Proto-Germanic *keluz.

From Middle Dutch kieme, kyme. Although the word is found as Old Dutch kīmo, it was probably borrowed from Middle Low German kīme, from Old Saxon kīmo because it did not undergo the regular change of -ī- to -ij- (so that *kijm would be expected). Possible influence of Latin cyma is also possible. Ul
From Middle Dutch crijt, from Middle Low German krît, a variant of Middle Low German krete, krêt, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kraitaz.
Possibly borrowed from Middle Low German krôch or its dialectal variant krûch. Cognate with German Krug.
From Middle Dutch leppe, with influence of Middle Low German lippe, from Old Dutch leppa, from Proto-West Germanic *lippjō.

From a borrowing of Middle Low German māt, māte, from Old Saxon *gimato, of West Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *gamatjô, itself from *ga- (“together”) + *matjô, from *matiz (“food”). Cognate with Old High German gimazzo, English mate.

parole.significato: a broker, notably in stocks and other financial products
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch makelare. By surface analysis, makelen + -aar, but the verb is thought to be secondary to this noun rather than the other way around (although the details are unclear). Middle Dutch makelare may in fact be borrowed from Middle Low German mēkeler. Compare German Makler.
Variant of miezelen, from Middle Dutch misel (“drizzle, mist”) or Middle Low German miseln, from Proto-Germanic *mihstaz (“fog, mist”) or Proto-Germanic *mīganą (“to urinate”). See English mizzle.
From Middle Low German mutte, perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“to be dirty, wet”).

parole.significato: moment, blink of an eye (instant of time)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ogenblic, from Middle Low German ōgenblik. Compare Norwegian øyeblikk, Danish øjeblik, German Augenblick, Icelandic augnablik, Swedish ögonblick, Yiddish אויגנבליק (oygnblik), and English eyeblink. Equivalent to oog (“eye”) + -en- + blik (“look”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German or Middle High German *ungestüemec, from Old High German *ungistuomi. See modern German ungestüm.
17th century, probably from Middle Low German pardûs, whence also German pardauz. Ultimately onomatopoeic. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål bardus, Swedish burdus, and Danish bardus.

parole.significato: poker (stick to kindle the fire in a fireplace)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch poke, poken or Middle Low German poken (both from Proto-Germanic *puk-), which is probably imitative. See also English poke.

parole.significato: an emissary from a city, almost exclusively from a Hanseatic city
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch râdessendebōde, from Middle Low German rādessendebōde. Equivalent to raad + -s- + zendbode. In modern usage influenced by and perhaps reoriginating from German Ratssendebote.

parole.significato: a rascal, a tomboy, a scamp
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German racker.

parole.significato: a ride on a mount (animal) or man-powered vehicle
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *rit, in Middle Dutch only sparsely attested in compounds, from Middle Low German rit or Middle High German ritt, related to Middle Dutch rêde, dialectal Dutch reed, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *rīdan.
Probably borrowed from Middle Low German rōrdump, from Old Saxon rōridumbil, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; cognates include Old English rāradumbla, Old High German rōratumbil.

Regional variant of schaper. Likely from an eastern dialect with umlaut on long vowels, such as Middle Low German schêper. Compare Low German Schaiper, German Schäfer. Alternatively directly from scheep, dialectal variant of schaap (apparently with spontaneous fronting).

parole.significato: a siskin, any member of the genus Spinus, or a closely-related small cardueline songbird
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch siseken, borrowed from Middle Low German sisek, from a Slavic language such as Czech číž. Cognate to English siskin.

parole.significato: slag (the impurities which result and are separated out when melting a metal or refining it from its ore)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slagge, whence also German Schlacke, English slag. See the latter.

Possibly from Middle Low German snake (“joker, prankster”), possible etymologically the same as Middle Low German snake (“viper, snake”) (see more at English snake). Possibly related to Dutch snakken (“to talk”).
From Middle Dutch stapelen, borrowed from Middle Low German stapelen, related to the noun stapel, from Old Saxon stapol (“basis, pillar, foundation”).
From Middle Dutch stocvisch, from Middle Low German [Term?]. Equivalent to stok + vis.

From Middle Dutch strepe, from Middle Low German strepe, from Proto-Germanic *stripō(n) or *straipō(n), of uncertain ultimate origin, perhaps derived from a lost strong verb *strīpaną, with no clear cognates outside of Germanic except for Irish sríab (“line, stripe”).
From Middle Dutch trueren, from Middle Low German truren, from Middle High German trūren (modern trauern).
Borrowed from Middle Low German trosse, from Old French trousse.

From Middle Dutch troye, from Middle Low German troie, troige, troge (“jacket, vest”) (also in Middle High German troie, treie, and Old Norse treyja (“jerkin, sleeveless jacket”)), from Old French troie (“doublet”), from Late Latin troja, troga (“horsehair monk's garment”), possibly originally of Tr

Probably from Middle Low German verlōf (“furlough, permission”) (possibly via or influenced by German Verlaub), from the verb verlōven (“to allow”), from Old Saxon far- + levian (“to give over, leave”). Cognate with English furlough, Danish forlov, German Verlaub (“permission”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German vut, from Old Saxon *fut, from Proto-West Germanic *futi (“vulva, uterus”).

From Middle Dutch vracht, from Middle Low German vracht, vrecht (“payment for cargo”), from Old Saxon frāht, frēht. Displaced the native Middle Dutch vrecht, both originally deriving from Proto-West Germanic *fra- + *aihti. Cognate with English freight and fraught.
Perhaps from Middle Low German villicht, villîcht (modern German Low German villicht). Cognate with German vielleicht.

In general use since the late 16th century, from Limburgish Middle Dutch vrēvel, Middle Low German vrēvel, and German Frevel, all from Proto-West Germanic *frafal(i). The spelling with wr- through association with unrelated wreed (“cruel, evil”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German sudeler, suteler.

From earlier swoel, probably from Middle Low German swōl, swūl (whence German Low German swool, German schwül), Old English swōl, swōliġ. Ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *swelan (“to burn”). More at sweal.

parole.significato: uvula (appendage that hangs from the palate)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch huch, huuch, huych, borrowed through Middle High German from Middle Low German hûk. Of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly borrowed from North Germanic, or possibly from a variant of Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ (“head covering”).

From earlier nerve, from Middle Dutch *narwe, either inherited from Old Dutch *narwa or borrowed from Middle Low German narwe, eventually from Proto-Germanic *narwō, from earlier *arwaz (“scar”). For the change of -rwe → -rf, compare verf. Cognate with German Narbe (“scar”).
From Middle Dutch pijler, pijlre, from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, either directly or via Middle Low German piler. Doublet of pilaar, which is a later borrowing from Medieval Latin.

parole.significato: a rope (often protected with wooden beads), chain or brace for fixing a spar to the mast
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *rak, from Old Dutch *rak, from Proto-West Germanic *rak, from Proto-Germanic *raką (“cord, chain”). Alternatively borrowed from Middle Low German rak (“parrel”), from Old Saxon *rak, from the same West Germanic source above.
